title: Why I Ran A 50K Through Rome Alone (And What It Taught Me)
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday recounts running 50 kilometers alone through Rome, stopping at Stoic sites such as the Column of Marcus Aurelius and the supposed tomb of Seneca. He opens with the irony that Marcus never saw his monument finished and that it was later rededicated to a different figure, which frames his argument that doing things for a trophy is a poor reason to do them. He prefers self-set challenges with no race, medal or official course because the reward is what he learns about himself. Along the way he gets lost, runs far slower than planned and nearly collapses near mile 29.5, using Seneca and Epictetus to explain preparing for difficulty and drawing on inner resources. He compares the late miles to finishing a book and closes with his young son joining him for the final stretch, concluding that the trophy was self-knowledge about his limits.
points: Holiday argues that challenges chosen for their own sake, with no medal or audience, build character better than competitions measured by external prizes.
Expecting a hard task to be harder than planned, as Seneca's line about the unexpected blow suggests, keeps setbacks like getting lost from becoming demoralizing.
Learning from someone who has done something similar, as he did with another long-distance runner, improved his preparation and his pacing.
Raising your threshold through repeated hard effort makes what once seemed like a lot feel like a little, and the real strength is earned after fatigue sets in.
The lasting reward of the run was knowing his limits and capacity, which no one can take away.
quotes: And doing hard things is good for you. That was the whole point. Do we do hard things because we want to impress people? Because we want to beat other people? Because we want a medal or a trophy?
That’s why I like doing challenges like this, more than races or competitions. There was no starting gun for this run, no official course, no medal waiting for me at the end.

When we do hard things, we have to be prepared for them to be harder than we’re anticipating. If you go into something thinking, This is all the gas I have in the tank. This is all I’m capable of doing. I need everything to go right, you’re in a really vulnerable position.
The point isn’t to win at your hobbies. The point is to do it, to have fun doing it, to experience it, to be there for it.
You push yourself, you raise your threshold higher and higher until what used to seem like a lot now only seems like a little.
At that point I was thinking about something Epictetus said: Whatever difficulties you face, understand what resources you have inside you.

Honestly, this is my favorite part. They say you’re not really pushing yourself until you get to your limits. It’s after you get tired and keep going that the muscle and strength and fortitude are earned.
I started the morning knowing I was going to try to run further than I ever had in my life. Six and a half hours later, I knew a little bit more about myself.
